meta.label: Broadband & internet
meta.attribution: Curated from public broadband labels, provider privacy policies, plan terms, network-management pages, and provider disclosures. Availability and pricing are address-specific; check your exact address, plan label, fees, and cancellation terms before switching. Suggest changes via Contribute.

reads.text: Compare broadband & internet by disclosure, fees, everyday access, and privacy.

axes.label: Fees or overall fit
axes.question: Lower fees or a stronger overall fit?

consumer.axes: Round 8 practical decision dials, with the S4 cost-or-values default where evidence permits.
consumer.budget: Round 8 honest budget eligibility, with S4 refusing to guess missing cost data.
consumer.archetypes: Round 8 computed answer slots matched to available category evidence.

products.name: Sonic Fiber
products.description: A California-focused fiber ISP with strong privacy posture, no data caps, no contracts, and unusually plain pricing where available.

privacy.note: Sonic says it minimizes data retention, including keeping dynamic IP and other log data for 0-14 days, and commits to EFF's Do Not Track policy.

fees.note: Sonic advertises free installation, no contracts, no data caps, and no confusing bundles on its fiber internet pages.

transparency.note: Sonic's residential internet page presents a simple single-service fiber offer rather than a bundle-heavy plan stack.

accessibility.note: Sonic's strongest fiber service is limited by local buildout, so address availability is the main constraint.

ethics.note: A short retention window, no data caps, and a privacy-forward public policy make Sonic a stronger values fit than most national ISPs where available.

products.name: NextLight
products.description: Longmont's city-owned fiber network, useful as a model for what transparent community broadband can look like.

privacy.note: NextLight publishes privacy and net-neutrality resources from its support/forms page and broadband-label links.

fees.note: NextLight markets no contracts, no data caps, no surprises, and community-owned service on its public plan pages.

transparency.note: NextLight publishes FCC-style broadband labels showing unlimited data and no additional data-usage charges.

accessibility.note: NextLight is excellent where Longmont serves you, but it is a city network rather than a national provider.

ethics.note: NextLight describes itself as community-owned, with decisions made locally rather than by a distant boardroom.

products.name: EPB Fiber Optics
products.description: Chattanooga's municipal-utility fiber network, with symmetrical fiber, no contracts, no hidden fees, and strong local-public value.

privacy.note: EPB publishes residential fiber legal documentation, including a privacy notice and acceptable-use materials.

fees.note: EPB advertises free installation, no contracts, no hidden fees, and plans starting at a clear monthly price.

transparency.note: EPB's internet pages state symmetrical fiber speeds, no data limits, and public plan information.

accessibility.note: EPB is strong inside its Chattanooga-area service territory but not broadly available outside it.

ethics.note: EPB is a public utility fiber provider, making accountability more local and public than national investor-owned ISPs.

products.name: Ting Internet
products.description: A fiber ISP in selected communities with simple pricing, no contracts, no installation fees, and unlimited data.

privacy.note: Ting's privacy policy explains collection, use, disclosure, and protection of customer and household personal information.

fees.note: Ting lists home fiber at a simple monthly price with no contracts, no installation fees, and no data limits or caps.

transparency.note: Ting's difference page foregrounds upfront pricing, no hidden fees, no contracts, and unlimited data.

accessibility.note: Ting is community-by-community fiber; availability is excellent in served addresses but limited nationally.

ethics.note: The no-contract, no-hidden-fee model is consumer-friendly, though Ting is still a private local fiber operator rather than a public utility.

products.name: Google Fiber
products.description: A fiber ISP with simple no-cap, no-contract plans where available, but tied to the wider Google data ecosystem.

privacy.note: GFiber publishes a dedicated privacy policy, but it remains part of the Google family and retains some data for business and legal purposes.

fees.note: Google Fiber advertises gigabit fiber plans with no data caps or contracts and public monthly pricing.

transparency.note: Google Fiber's plan and support pages state no data caps and no contracts in plain public documentation.

accessibility.note: Google Fiber availability is still city- and address-dependent rather than nationwide.

ethics.note: No caps and no contracts are positive, while platform-family privacy concerns keep the public-interest score below municipal fiber.

products.name: Frontier Fiber
products.description: A regional fiber and broadband provider with no-data-cap fiber messaging and public broadband labels, strongest where the fiber network is available.

privacy.note: Frontier's policy page notes that it does not track or sell individual browsing history.

fees.note: Frontier says its internet plans come with unlimited data and no data caps or overage charges.

transparency.note: Frontier publishes FCC Broadband Consumer Labels for fees, promotional pricing, and product details.

accessibility.note: Frontier serves many regions, but quality and speed depend heavily on whether the address gets fiber rather than legacy service.

ethics.note: No-cap fiber and an explicit no-browsing-history claim are positives, though Frontier remains an investor-owned regional telecom.

products.name: Verizon Home Internet
products.description: A mainstream fiber and fixed-wireless provider with broad access, good disclosure pages, and the privacy/accountability tradeoffs of a major telecom.

privacy.note: Verizon's privacy policy describes broad collection, use, sharing, and advertising choices across Verizon services.

fees.note: Verizon publishes Broadband Facts labels for home internet plans, but labels do not include all discounts, offers, or perks.

transparency.note: Verizon's consumer broadband labels provide plan pricing and technical details in the FCC label format.

accessibility.note: Verizon combines Fios and 5G/LTE home routes, giving more address options than a fiber-only provider.

ethics.note: Clear labels help, but the major-telecom data model and Verizon's 2024 FCC wireless location-data fine weigh against accountability.

products.name: T-Mobile Home Internet
products.description: A widely available 5G home internet option with simple setup and no annual contract, but weaker fit for privacy and wired-fiber reliability.

privacy.note: T-Mobile's privacy notice covers extensive personal, account, device, location, CPNI, advertising, and sharing practices.

fees.note: T-Mobile Home Internet advertises no annual contract and no monthly equipment fees, but taxes and fees can be excluded.

transparency.note: T-Mobile states price-guarantee and equipment terms publicly, while exclusions such as taxes and fees still require attention.

accessibility.note: 5G home service can reach addresses that lack fiber or cable choice, but it is approved only where T-Mobile determines a good experience.

ethics.note: No annual contract helps, but T-Mobile's 2024 FCC wireless location-data fine weighs against parent-company accountability.

products.name: AT&T Fiber
products.description: A widely recognized fiber provider with real high-speed value where fiber is installed, but a major-telecom privacy and fee tradeoff.

privacy.note: AT&T's privacy notice applies to internet, wireless, voice, apps, data use, advertising choices, and customer privacy controls.

fees.note: AT&T says Broadband Facts monthly prices do not include offers, promotions, or government taxes and itemize location-based fees.

transparency.note: AT&T publishes machine-readable Broadband Facts for current plans, improving fee and plan inspectability.

accessibility.note: AT&T has broad national recognition and fiber buildout, but the best experience depends on address-level fiber availability.

ethics.note: Fiber availability is useful, but AT&T's 2024 FCC wireless location-data fine and broad data model weigh against accountability.

products.name: Spectrum Internet
products.description: A widely available cable ISP with no home-internet data caps, but weaker privacy and public-accountability fit than local fiber.

privacy.note: Spectrum's privacy policy and privacy-rights pages describe customer data collection, marketing choices, and advertising opt-outs.

fees.note: Spectrum states it does not impose data caps on home internet plans and advertises no hidden fees on its internet page.

transparency.note: Spectrum posts plan and data-cap claims publicly, but pricing and actual speeds still vary by area and restrictions.

accessibility.note: Spectrum's cable footprint gives broad availability in served markets and an easier address match than local-only fiber.

ethics.note: No data caps are a positive, but Spectrum remains a large cable ISP with a broad privacy and advertising-choice regime rather than local public ownership.

products.name: Xfinity Internet
products.description: A very widely available Comcast service with official broadband labels and current no-cap messaging, but a weaker fit for privacy and simplicity values.

privacy.note: Xfinity's privacy policy explains the personal information Comcast collects, uses, maintains, protects, and shares.

fees.note: Xfinity says current internet plans have unlimited data, while broadband disclosures and plan labels still need checking for local fees and terms.

transparency.note: Xfinity publishes broadband disclosures and Broadband Facts labels for current plans in a downloadable machine-readable format.

accessibility.note: Comcast/Xfinity has one of the broadest cable footprints, making it available where many smaller values-aligned providers are not.

ethics.note: Broad availability and labels help, but the large cable-company privacy model and complex disclosure stack make this an honest floor entry.

products.name: Cox Internet
products.description: A regional cable ISP with broad local availability in many markets, but weaker scoring because base plans can still carry data allowances.

privacy.note: Cox's annual privacy notice explains collection, use, and disclosure of personally identifiable information in connection with services.

fees.note: Cox says internet plans come with a 1.25 TB monthly data allowance and unlimited data can require an additional plan or qualifying bundle.

transparency.note: Cox publishes internet service disclosures and Broadband Facts guidance, but users still need to inspect data limits and add-on terms.

accessibility.note: Cox is available in many cable markets, but service quality and competition vary by address.

ethics.note: A data allowance with paid unlimited-data pathways makes Cox a weaker fit for simplicity and consumer-fairness values.
